notes.111r.46: 'andro lydha' (111r.46) is read as 'obey another'; the sense is uncertain. 'eer' (111v.11) is taken as bronze or brass.
notes.113r.12: 'mere mon' (113r.15) is taken as 'greater things'. 'et ynia' (113r.34) is unclear; taken as 'a little favour'. 'lofwa' (113r.42) may mean 'praise' or 'promise'.

nodes.text: Will you mark and listen
to what the heathens could do in former days?
You will not understand it well
unless you keep it with wit and reason.
Of King Alexander I will tell;
what the writing says I will not keep silent.
In twelve years he won the world for himself;
how water and weather shall obey another,
they know all that shall befall them,
either good or ill.
As I read in the writing
of a king who was called Nectanebus:
within he was all full of devilry,
though outwardly he shone like gold.
He was told of it at once
that King Artaxerxes was making ready
to come from Persia in full strength
and visit Nectanebus in the land of Egypt,
and meant to capture and conquer Nectanebus
then straight away, at that same time.
When Nectanebus learned these tidings,
he went secretly into his palace,
took a basin made all of bronze,
filled it with water till it held no more;
there he showed his devil's craft.
because he had thought it over beforehand.
Philip wants to keep you and love you,
and to believe no false tongue.
Yet greater things shall befall you:
you shall soon be with a young son.
The god Ammon shall come to you;
he has his secret judgments.
He is like a middle-aged man;
of middling size, so is he,
like a god and not like a man.
You shall not fear him at all.
He has horns just like a sheep,
his beard grey, and his hair as well.
He will come to you soon,
as soon as you first sleep tonight.
When you two have had joy and pleasure,
you are with a son; so I have learned.
As I understand a woman's mind,
it often lies to her;
fickleness and the wayward mind
make most women soft;
whoever asks kindly, they cannot refuse;
a man can lure one with a little favour.
Women ought gladly to keep quiet
and not ask all they please;
whoever asks much gets an answer.
Queen Olympias took heed of this,
of the words the master had told her;
she answers well and could not keep silent:
If what you have promised me comes true,
before God I will praise you as is right.
Nectanebus laughed heartily to himself
[when] he heard the queen speak so.
So he bade her good night,
went off where he worked his art right skilfully
with devilry and his master's leave.
It seemed to the queen, as soon as she slept,
that the god Ammon lay with her,
as Nectanebus had told of,
and told her in her dreams:
You are with a son; he shall judge
right and wrong among all people.
Then she wakes, bade [them] fetch her interpreter,
Nectanebus, and told [him] thus
all that she saw in the dream,
asked him to tell her when it shall happen
that the god Ammon will show himself to me.
Nectanebus was very cunning;
he gave her this answer:
Tonight he comes as a dragon;
lady, then he will be your mate.
First he turns into a man;
into my shape he then changes,
and afterwards you shall find all that [true]
which I have read in your dreams.
Nectanebus won her for himself;
the god Ammon knew nothing of such deceit.
That night, in the first sleep,
there came a dragon, shining all green;
it became a man and lay there quiet;
it was Nectanebus himself.
They lay a while, each in the other's arms;
then he went back into his own shape.
